title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (fixed on the previous page and summarised on the next): X is a smooth projective variety of dimension n, Y a smooth hyperplane section, and U = X − Y the affine complement. A^i_r(X) is the Chow group (rational equivalence) and A^i_a(X) the group modulo algebraic equivalence. The superscript I read as τ (the next page writes it J^* = A^*_r(X)^a) is the subgroup of rational classes that are algebraically equivalent to zero, the 'continuous' or Jacobian part. 'exc. p' means 'except for p-torsion' (characteristic p). 'mod gr. finis' means 'up to finite groups'. 'id' in the third column means 'idem' (same as the line above), not 'identity'. E is intersection with the hyperplane class.

Grothendieck is running a test table: a package of Lefschetz-type conjectures for Chow groups, checked dimension by dimension. Each candidate statement is marked OK (known or follows from known results), '?' or '??'. Pencil arrows link the open questions.

The package has four parts:
(1) Weak Lefschetz for restriction A^i(X) → A^i(Y): bijective in low codimension, injective in the middle codimension.
(2) Weak Lefschetz for Gysin push-forward A_i(Y) → A_i(X): bijective or surjective for small dimension i.
(2') Vanishing of the low-dimensional Chow groups of the affine complement U.
(3) Hard Lefschetz for cycles.
  - Modulo algebraic equivalence: E^{n-2i}: A^i_a(X) → A^{n-i}_a(X), bijective modulo finite groups.
  - For the algebraically trivial part, with the index shift of odd cohomology H^{2i-1}: E^{n-2i+1}: A^i_r(X)^τ → A^{n-i+1}_r(X)^τ.

Top of the page (end of the n=3 case, τ-part):
- E^4: A^0^τ → A^4^τ. Both sides are 0, so OK.
- E^2: A^1^τ = Pic^0 → A^3^τ (degree-0 zero-cycles). OK only if rational equivalence on 0-cycles equals Albanese equivalence: Pic^0 is isogenous to Alb by Lefschetz.
- id: A^2^τ → A^2^τ. OK.
- (2') A_0(U) = 0, A_1^a(U) = 0 (exc. p), marked '??'.

n = 4:
- (1) A^0 restriction is Z = Z, OK. A^1 restriction Pic X → Pic Y is bijective, OK: this is Grothendieck–Lefschetz, SGA 2, since dim Y = 3. Restriction A^2_r(X)^τ → A^2_r(Y)^τ injective is marked '?', the 'continuous question'.
- (2) A_0(Y) → A_0(X) bijective (the page has a slip, writing X for Y). OK provided rational equivalence = Albanese equivalence on 0-cycles, since Alb Y ≅ Alb X. A_1(Y) → A_1(X) surjective: '?'. Its τ-part: '?', continuous question. A_1^a(Y) → A_1^a(X) bijective: '?', 'numerical question (essentially)'.
- (3) Modulo algebraic equivalence: E^4 on A^0 → A^4 (Z ≅ Z) OK; E^2: A^1_a → A^3_a 'idem' with no OK; id on A^2_a, OK.
- (3), τ-part: E^5: 0 → 0, OK. E^3: Pic^0 → A_0^0 OK only if rational equivalence = Albanese equivalence. E: A^2^τ → A^3^τ '?', continuous question.
- (2') A_0(U) = A_1(U) = 0 exc. p, marked '??'.

The pencil arrows record the logical structure. The hard-Lefschetz map E: A^2 → A^3 factors as restriction A^2(X) → A^2(Y) = A_1(Y) followed by push-forward A_1(Y) → A_1(X) = A^3(X). So the hard-Lefschetz question on the continuous part is linked to:
- injectivity of restriction (τ-part), and
- surjectivity of push-forward (τ-part).
Likewise E^2 on A^1_a is linked to bijectivity of A_1^a(Y) → A_1^a(X), which he labels essentially a numerical question, i.e. whether algebraic equivalence agrees with numerical equivalence modulo torsion.

In short, the hard Lefschetz theorem for cycles is broken into a 'numerical' part (algebraic equivalence) and a 'continuous' part (algebraically trivial cycles), each reduced to weak-Lefschetz statements for a hyperplane section.
errors: (2) for n=4 is written 'A^r_0(X) — A^r_0(X)'; it should be A^r_0(Y) → A^r_0(X). This is a slip.

For E^{n-1}: Pic^0(X) → A_0(X)^τ, Grothendieck correctly adds the condition that rational equivalence = Albanese equivalence on 0-cycles. Without it the statement is false by Mumford (1969): the Albanese kernel is huge when p_g > 0 over C.

For the same reason, (2') A_0(U) = 0 for the affine complement fails over C whenever H^{n,0}(X) ≠ 0. A_0(U) = 0 is equivalent to A_0(Y) → A_0(X) being surjective, which Mumford/Roitman and Bloch–Srinivas rule out. His '??' is justified. Over an algebraically closed field of transcendence degree 0 this is only conjecturally true (it would follow from Bloch–Beilinson), rationally.

Hard Lefschetz modulo algebraic equivalence (E^{n-2i}: A^i_a ⊗ Q → A^{n-i}_a ⊗ Q bijective mod finite groups), labelled 'conjecture raisonnable' on the previous page for n=3 and 'question numérique' here, is false. Griffiths (1969) found homologically trivial 1-cycles on threefolds that are not algebraically trivial, and Clemens showed the Griffiths group can be infinitely generated. Images of the finitely generated NS(X) cannot fill A^{n-1}_a ⊗ Q. Grothendieck's own identification of this as essentially 'algebraic = numerical equivalence' is exactly where it breaks.
The bijectivity of A_1^a(Y) → A_1^a(X) for n=4 fails for the same Griffiths-group reasons.

ideas.what: Weak Lefschetz for Chow groups: restriction CH^i(X) → CH^i(Y) to an ample smooth hyperplane section is an isomorphism (mod torsion / rationally) in low codimension and injective in the middle, alongside a dual push-forward statement CH_i(Y) → CH_i(X).
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz (hyperplane) conjecture for Chow groups; Hartshorne's question
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hartshorne (1975, 'Equivalence relations on algebraic cycles and subvarieties of small codimension'); later seen as a consequence of the Bloch–Beilinson–Murre conjectures; partial results by Paranjape (1994) and others
ideas.where_published: Pic case: SGA 2 (Grothendieck–Lefschetz). General Chow-group form: not to my knowledge.

ideas.what: Hard Lefschetz for cycles modulo algebraic equivalence: E^{n-2i}: A^i_a(X) → A^{n-i}_a(X) bijective modulo finite groups, recognised as essentially a numerical question.
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz standard conjecture B transposed to algebraic equivalence; would imply algebraic = numerical equivalence (false by Griffiths)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck's standard conjectures (1969) and Kleiman (1968) for homological/numerical equivalence; the counterexample is Griffiths (1969)
ideas.where_published: 'Standard conjectures on algebraic cycles' (Bombay 1968/1969) treats homological/numerical equivalence; I am unsure whether the algebraic-equivalence variant is stated there.

ideas.what: Shifted hard Lefschetz for algebraically trivial cycles: E^{n-2i+1}: CH^i(X)_alg → CH^{n-i+1}(X)_alg (the index shift of H^{2i-1}). Expected to hold only after replacing rational equivalence by a coarser 'Albanese / intermediate-Jacobian' equivalence.
ideas.modern_name: Lefschetz isogeny for algebraic representatives Ab^i(X) → Ab^{n-i+1}(X) (intermediate algebraic Jacobians)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Murre (algebraic representatives, 1980s); Vial ('Projectors on the intermediate algebraic Jacobians', ~2013) for some cases

ideas.what: Decomposition of the cycle-theoretic hard Lefschetz map E as restriction to Y followed by Gysin push-forward from Y. The 'continuous' and 'numerical' open questions are each reduced to a weak-Lefschetz injectivity/surjectivity pair, recorded by the pencil arrows.
ideas.modern_name: Standard reduction of hard Lefschetz to the hyperplane case, applied to Chow groups split into Griffiths/Néron–Severi part and Abel–Jacobi part
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical in cohomology (Lefschetz); for Chow groups implicit in Bloch–Beilinson / Murre filtration literature

ideas.what: Vanishing of the low-dimensional Chow groups CH_0(U), CH_1(U) of the affine complement U = X − Y, marked '??'.
ideas.modern_name: Chow groups of affine varieties (Murthy-type questions; Bloch–Srinivas decomposition of the diagonal)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Murthy, Roitman (torsion of CH_0 of affine varieties), Bloch–Srinivas (1983)

ideas.what: Recognition that the Lefschetz property Pic^0 → CH_0^0 holds only if rational equivalence of 0-cycles equals Albanese equivalence.
ideas.modern_name: Bloch's conjecture / Albanese kernel; Mumford's infinite-dimensionality theorem

missed.claim: Grothendieck (between 1965 and about 1971) set out a systematic test-table of Lefschetz-type conjectures for Chow groups: weak Lefschetz for restriction and push-forward, vanishing for the affine complement, and hard Lefschetz. Each was split into a 'numerical' part (algebraic equivalence) and a 'continuous' part (algebraically trivial cycles, with the shifted exponent E^{n-2i+1}). This predates Hartshorne's 1975 formulation and the Bloch–Beilinson/Murre framework, and is not credited to him.
missed.quote: A^2_r(X)^τ — A^2_r(Y)^τ injectif exc. p ? — question "continue" ... A^a_1(Y) → A^a_1(X) bij. exc. p. ? question "numérique" (ess.t)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is historical priority for the 'Lefschetz conjecture for Chow groups' and the numerical/continuous dichotomy. The continuous hard-Lefschetz question for codimension-2 algebraically trivial cycles on a fourfold (E: A^2^τ → A^3^τ, up to an Albanese-type equivalence) is close to what Vial and others study for algebraic representatives.

missed.claim: Grothendieck explicitly ties the hard-Lefschetz question modulo algebraic equivalence to 'algebraic equivalence = numerical equivalence', a link later shown false by Griffiths. He also isolates the condition 'rational = Albanese equivalence on 0-cycles' needed for the continuous part, anticipating Mumford/Bloch.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mostly historical. It documents that Grothendieck saw these obstructions as the key open points in a Chow-level Lefschetz programme.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an informal checklist, but it shows Grothendieck formulating Chow-group Lefschetz conjectures (weak and hard, numerical vs continuous, with the correct shifted exponent for the Jacobian part) years before Hartshorne and Bloch–Beilinson. He correctly locates the Albanese obstruction. Several of the hoped-for statements are now known false (Griffiths, Mumford), and the ideas are well developed in later literature, so the novelty is mainly historical priority.
transcription_corrections: The superscript transcribed as ^{\mathbb{Q}} is ^τ (the algebraically-trivial part, J^* = A^*_r(X)^a of the next page), not rational coefficients. Consistent with this, A^0_r(X)^τ = 0.
The marks under the first line are '≃0' (both A^0^τ and A^4^τ vanish), not 'wr'.
The top block (E^4: A^0^τ → A^4^τ, E^2: A^1^τ → A^3^τ, id on A^2^τ) is the τ-part of the n=3 case from the previous page, using exponent E^{n-2i+1}. Likewise the n=4 τ-rows use E^5, E^3, E.
'id' in the third column means 'idem' (same as above), e.g. 'bij. mod gr. finis'.
The top-right margin reads roughly 'si équiv. [crossed out] = équiv. Alb' (Albanese equivalence), not 'équiv. alg.'.
The n=4 (2) margin reads 'si équiv. rat.(?) = équiv. Alb'.
The first line's comment is 'bijective mod gr. finis'.
The pencil annotation near (3) for n=4 reads 'mod groupes finis' and belongs to the arrow linking E^2: A^1_a → A^3_a with the 'question numérique' line.
The 'A^a_1' in the first (2') is transcribed as written, though it may be A^r_1.
